f: Owners seeking greater precision have two main routes: a boundary agreement or a determined boundary.
A boundary agreement can address the position of the legal boundary.
A boundary agreement can also address maintenance of a boundary feature.
There is a rebuttable presumption that a boundary agreement does not transfer land.
The agreed position is presumed to coincide with the true legal boundary unless rebutted.
Where an agreed position differs from a title plan, it can identify the current legal boundary only within the general-boundaries rule.
A substantial transfer of land should normally be completed by formal transfer or conveyance.
An agreement demarcating an unclear boundary can bind successors in title.
A simple boundary agreement without a disposing purpose need not be written to be enforceable.
HM Land Registry guidance recommends putting a boundary agreement in writing and signing it.
There is no prescribed form for a written boundary agreement.
Parties and witnesses should sensibly sign and date an attached boundary plan.
A precise, high-quality plan makes the agreement more useful to parties and successors.
In some cases a boundary can be identified adequately by words without a plan.
A mortgagee will not generally need to be a party to a simple boundary agreement.
A boundary agreement can be recorded in the individual registered titles.
Recording requires the appropriate correction or alteration of register transaction.
A copy of the boundary agreement must be uploaded with the alteration application.
The prescribed register-alteration fee must be paid.
A registered chargee may be notified if not a party and consent is not lodged.
A recorded boundary agreement does not itself convert a general boundary into a determined boundary.
Recording an agreement does not guarantee that the legal boundary is at the agreed position.
A determined-boundary application is required to show the exact line for register purposes.
Before applying, the exact line must be identified from available evidence.
The exact line must be identified by a plan or by a plan plus verbal description.
The plan must show enough surrounding features to locate its general position on OS mapping.
All adjoining owners and service addresses must be identified.
For notice purposes, owners include registered charge holders.
Unregistered adjoining land requires documentary title evidence.
A third party may own a strip between apparently adjoining red-edged title plans.
Only one Determined Boundary transaction is required regardless of the number of adjoining boundaries.
The registrar checks exact-line identification, an arguable case, and identification of all adjoining owners.
Notice is generally served unless written adjoining-owner agreement or a court order is lodged.
The application must be cancelled if the registrar is not satisfied on the required tests.
An expert report may bind instructing parties but is not conclusive for the registrar.
A non-groundless objection is referred to the First-tier Tribunal unless agreement is reached.
Determined boundaries are normally surveyed by permanent-feature measurements or National Grid coordinates.
National Grid coordinate surveying requires specialist equipment and is likely more expensive.
The preferred determined-boundary plan scale is no smaller than 1:200.
A determined-boundary plan should ideally be no larger than A3.
The plan must not include a disclaimer casting doubt on its accuracy.
Measurements on a determined-boundary plan must be accurate to plus or minus 10 mm.
Measurements must be horizontal rather than taken along a slope.
Measurements must use at least two defined points on permanent physical features.
A permanent reference feature should reasonably remain in position for at least ten years.
Accepted National Grid coordinates require absolute accuracy of plus or minus 300 mm.
Accepted National Grid coordinates require relative accuracy of plus or minus 10 mm.
Wooden hubs or stakes are not accepted as permanent ground markers.
Planning data must be published on the authority's official website.
Published data must use a clear and understandable format.
CSV is an accepted publication format.
GeoJSON is an accepted publication format.
GML is an accepted publication format.
GeoPackage is an accepted publication format.
The webpage must state that the data is provided under the Open Government Licence.
An endpoint can be a hosted downloadable file.
An endpoint can be a live API feed.
An ArcGIS endpoint includes a numeric layer identifier.
Updates should be made at the existing endpoint URL rather than changing it.
The dataset webpage must link to the endpoint URL.
The dataset webpage must summarise what the data covers.
Each record's documentation-url must be unique.
A unique documentation URL can use one webpage per record.
Multiple records may share a page if each uses a unique anchor fragment.
Publishers must check that their system supports anchor links.
Legal-document records require a document-url linking directly to the file.
Providing data requires both endpoint and source-webpage URLs.
The platform updates automatically when the existing endpoint content changes.
A new endpoint URL requires the data to be provided again.
Article 4 directions require separate direction and direction-area datasets.
The direction dataset needs at least one row per direction.
Direction references must be unique within the provider dataset.
Direction references must remain stable across updates.
The name field contains the official direction name.
document-url points to the authoritative order or notice.
documentation-url points to a webpage introducing the document.
end-date remains blank while the direction is active.
The area dataset needs at least one row per direction area.
Area references must be unique within the provider dataset.
Area references must remain stable across updates.
Area geometry is a polygon or multipolygon.
CSV area geometry is encoded as WKT.
UPRN and address-text must be supplied together when used.
The article-4-direction field links an area to its direction reference.
WCS is an OGC standard for serving and retrieving multidimensional coverages.
WCS can be consumed in QGIS and Esri ArcGIS Desktop.
WCS can return raw pixel values such as elevation.
WCS is available for LIDAR Composite elevation models.
WCS is available for the SurfZone DEM.
WCS is available for the Vegetation Object Model.
WCS and WMS provide a non-proprietary alternative to Esri image services.
The publisher documents compatibility issues with WCS in ArcGIS.
ArcGIS WCS does not automatically support raster statistics.
ArcGIS elevation rasters may require stretch rendering.
The published DTM 1 m minimum statistic is -409.05.
The published DTM 1 m maximum statistic is 978.05.
The published DTM 1 m mean statistic is 104.63.
The published DTM 1 m standard deviation is 107.52.
WCS GeoTIFF NoData is encoded as -3.4028235e+38.
NoData is represented numerically because GeoTIFF contains a two-dimensional numeric array.
The 1 m composite DTM covers approximately 99 percent of England.
The DTM removes protruding surface objects to represent terrain.
The DTM uses the last or only laser return.
The current composite was produced in 2022.
The composite combines Time Stamped and National LIDAR Programme surveys.
Repeated coverage uses the newest best-resolution survey.
Resampled source data uses bilinear interpolation.
The composite is supplied as GeoTIFF.
Downloads are organised in 5 km OS National Grid tiles.
The vertical datum is Ordnance Survey Newlyn.
Input survey vertical accuracy is plus or minus 15 cm RMSE.
The horizontal coordinate system is EPSG:27700.
The composite update frequency is annual.
The dataset is licensed under the Open Government Licence.
Published point-density figures are calculated for DSM returns.
A 1 m DSM averages at least one point per square metre.
A 50 cm DSM averages four points per square metre.
A 25 cm DSM averages sixteen points per square metre.
DTM density below vegetation may be lower than nominal DSM density.
LIDAR point clouds are not regular grids.
Overlapping flight lines can increase point density.
OS Terrain 50 is an open height dataset for Great Britain.
The product is updated annually in July.
The product is published as both grid and contour data.
Grid and contour products are created from the same source data.
Tiled data uses 10 km by 10 km National Grid tiles.
Tile identifiers use the southwest National Grid reference.
The grid uses regular 50 m post spacing.
Standard contour polylines use 10 m intervals.
Contours include mean high and mean low water boundaries.
The tiled national product contains 2,858 tiles.
The tiled product is arranged into 55 folders.
Each folder represents a 100 km grid square.
GeoPackage contours are supplied as a single national file.
Vector tiles are supplied as a single national MBTiles file.
The product is maintained through annual full-tile resupply.
A full national grid supply is about 157 MB compressed.
Zip-compressed product data is not encrypted.
Grid heights are calculated at pixel centres.
Grid construction has no overlap or common edge values between tiles.
Mean-water grid heights use a tile-average value derived from local tide tables.
Adjacent coastal tiles may contain a small discrete tidal-height step.
Foreshore heights are interpolated between mean high and low water.
Contour features are supplied as polylines.
Contour GML stores heights in the INSPIRE propertyValue attribute.
Shapefile field names are constrained to ten characters.
Contour classes master and ordinary correspond to index and standard contours.
Each tiled GML contour supply includes a per-tile metadata XML file.
Spot heights are automatically selected from the highest mass point inside a closed contour.
A spot height equal to its enclosing contour is removed.
A spot height may be lower than the surrounding contour where a genuine depression exists.
Spot-height z values are rounded to zero decimal places.
GeoPackage contour layers are spot_height, land_water_boundary and contour_line.
GeoPackage attribute names are not restricted to short lengths.
Vector tiles use Web Mercator EPSG:3857.
Core vector-tile attributes are mapped from zoom levels 9 through 14.
XML metadata follows the GEMINI standard.
OS publishes XML schema resources for contour, grid and viewing-style metadata.
